claims.text: The relevant nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and are initially crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
Configurational entropy from approximately equimolar multielement mixing can stabilize a solid-solution phase.
Stability over 473–1923 K is governed by a balance between entropic stabilization and temperature-activated atomic diffusion.
Increasing temperature activates atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
Atomic diffusion promotes local elemental segregation, secondary-phase formation, and phase instability.
At lower temperatures, high configurational entropy maintains the solid-solution state.
As temperature rises, kinetic energy overcomes entropic mixing stabilization.
A critical temperature threshold exists above which segregation or phase separation compromises stability.
Below the critical threshold, diffraction patterns and elemental distributions remain stable and uniform.
Above the critical threshold, lattice parameters change and secondary diffraction peaks emerge.
Above the critical threshold, local elemental segregation becomes detectable.
Above the critical threshold, oxidation-state shifts may occur.
The initial state at approximately 473 K has a homogeneous elemental distribution and stable single-phase diffraction pattern.
The prediction is intended to hold during temperature cycling from 473 K to 1923 K under controlled inert or reducing atmospheres.
Residual oxygen can alter the observed stability through unintended oxidation.
The critical temperature and diffusion activation energy depend on nanoparticle size, elemental combination, and ambient conditions.
A sample held at 473 K for the same duration provides the controlled baseline for the temperature-ramped sample.
Retention of a uniform solid solution with no detectable lattice, phase-purity, or elemental-distribution changes near 1923 K would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis does not establish that the critical threshold must lie below 1923 K, and the uncertainty field leaves its value unspecified, yet the falsification rule treats the absence of change by 1923 K as decisive. The proposed balance could instead favor the solid solution throughout the tested range.
